name: Indra Jatra, Kathmandu
when: September, around the full moon of the Newar month of Yenla (lunar); about eight days
summary: Kathmandu's biggest street festival marks the end of the monsoon. A tall wooden pole is raised outside Hanuman Dhoka, masked Lakhey dancers work the lanes, the Seto Bhairav mask is uncovered, and the living goddess Kumari rides through the old city in a wooden chariot.
body: Indra Jatra belongs to the Newars of Kathmandu and honours Indra, the Vedic king of the gods and bringer of rain, at the moment the monsoon ends and the rice is ripening. It opens with the raising of the yosin, a long wooden pole brought from the forest and set upright in front of the old palace at Hanuman Dhoka. A banner of Indra hangs from it for the length of the festival, and its lowering on the last night closes the celebration.

The part most visitors come for is Kumari Jatra. The Kumari, a young Newar girl worshipped as a living goddess, leaves the Kumari Ghar on Durbar Square and is pulled through the old city in a wooden chariot, followed by smaller chariots carrying boys who represent Ganesh and Bhairav. The chariot procession was added to Indra Jatra in the eighteenth century under Jaya Prakash Malla, the last Malla king of Kathmandu. The routes change on different days, covering the lower, upper and middle parts of the old town.

Around the processions, Durbar Square becomes a stage. Masked dancers perform each evening, the red-faced Lakhey demon dances through the lanes, and the large gilded mask of Seto (White) Bhairav near Hanuman Dhoka is uncovered for the festival days. The Nepali head of state traditionally attends on the main day to receive a tika from the Kumari. Dates follow the lunar calendar and processions run late; check current status before you travel.
tips: Find a step or a terrace café on Durbar Square at least an hour before the chariot leaves; the crowd packs in fast.
Do not use flash on the Kumari or her chariot, and do not try to touch it or block its path.
Buy the Durbar Square ticket in advance or keep your SAARC ID handy; checks continue through the festival.

faqs.a: Indra Jatra follows the Newar lunar calendar and usually falls in September, lasting about eight days around the full moon of the month of Yenla. The pole-raising opens it and the main Kumari chariot day follows a few days later. Exact dates move each year, so check current status before you travel and book a room near Durbar Square early.

faqs.q: Where is the best place to watch the Kumari chariot?
faqs.a: Kathmandu Durbar Square, near the Kumari Ghar and Hanuman Dhoka, where the chariot procession begins. Rooftop cafés around the square sell seats or charge high minimum spends on the main day. Arrive at least an hour early, keep valuables in a front pocket and stay out of the chariot's path, because the wheels do not stop for spectators.

faqs.q: Is Indra Jatra safe for families and solo women?
faqs.a: Yes, it is a family festival and very public, but the crowds on the main evening are dense. Keep children close and agree a meeting point. Solo women are generally fine in the square; as in any big crowd, stay near families and stalls, avoid the tightest pushes near the chariot and leave by the wider lanes towards New Road.

faqs.q: Do I need a ticket for Kathmandu Durbar Square during the festival?
faqs.a: Yes, the Durbar Square heritage entry fee applies to tourists through the year, including festival days. SAARC nationals, including Indians, pay a lower rate than other foreigners on showing ID. Fees are revised from time to time, so check current status before you travel and keep your ticket with you for re-entry.

name: Bisket Jatra, Bhaktapur
when: Mid-April, around Nepali New Year (1 Baisakh); about nine days
summary: Bhaktapur's new-year festival runs for about nine days in mid-April. Huge chariots of Bhairav and Bhadrakali are hauled through the old town in a tug-of-war between its upper and lower halves, and a tall pole raised at Yoshin Khel is pulled down to mark the turn of the Nepali year.
body: Bisket Jatra is Bhaktapur's festival, and it runs on the solar new year of the Bikram Sambat calendar, Nepal's official calendar, which begins on 1 Baisakh in mid-April. It starts in Taumadhi Square below the five-tiered Nyatapola temple, where the three-roofed chariot of Bhairav is assembled. Teams from the upper and lower halves of the town take the ropes at either end and pull against each other; whichever side wins drags the chariot into its own quarter, and that is read as good luck for the year.

Over the next days the chariots of Bhairav and the smaller one of his consort Bhadrakali move down towards the riverside ground at Yoshin Khel. There a tall wooden pole, the yosin, is raised with long banners. On the evening before New Year it is pulled down, again in a contest between the two halves of the town, and the year turns when it falls. The pulling is rough and fast and every year people are hurt, so watch from a distance.

Neighbouring Thimi and Bode hold their own new-year jatras at the same time, with portable shrines and red powder thrown in the streets. For visitors, Bisket Jatra is the best time to see Bhaktapur's Newar neighbourhoods acting as a community, with feasting in every house. It also fills the town's guesthouses. Dates follow the official calendar, so check current status before you travel.
tips: Watch the tug-of-war from a temple plinth or rooftop on Taumadhi Square, never from the street in front of the wheels.
Book a guesthouse inside the old town early; it is far easier than taxiing in from Kathmandu through festival traffic.
Keep the Bhaktapur entry ticket with you; it is valid for several days if you register your passport at the ticket office.

faqs.q: When is Bisket Jatra in Bhaktapur?
faqs.a: It is tied to Nepali New Year, 1 Baisakh in the Bikram Sambat calendar, which usually falls on 13 or 14 April. The festival begins a few days earlier and lasts about nine days, with the pole felled on the eve of New Year. The chariot pulls run on set days, so check current status before you travel and plan two nights.

faqs.q: Is Bisket Jatra dangerous to watch?
faqs.a: The chariot pulling is rough, crowded and fast, and injuries happen most years among participants and people standing too close. Watching from steps, plinths or rooftops around Taumadhi Square is safe enough. Keep children back, do not stand in front of the wheels or on the downhill side, and leave when the crowd surges towards the ropes.

faqs.q: Can I do Bisket Jatra as a day trip from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Yes, Bhaktapur is 15 km from Thamel, about an hour by taxi or local bus. But the most interesting pulls happen in the evening and traffic is heavy, so staying one or two nights in the old town is better. You then also see the morning rituals and the quieter neighbourhood feasts.

faqs.q: How much is the Bhaktapur entry fee during Bisket Jatra?
faqs.a: The normal heritage fee applies: NPR 500 for SAARC visitors, including Indians, and NPR 1,800 for other foreigners in recent years. Register your passport at the ticket office if you want to use the same ticket for more than one day. Fees change from time to time; check current status before you travel.

name: Tiji Festival, Lo Manthang
image_query: Tiji festival Lo Manthang masked dance
when: May, usually three days in the third Tibetan month (lunar)
summary: Tiji is Upper Mustang's three-day spring festival of masked dances in the walled town of Lo Manthang. Monks of the Sakya tradition perform in the square below the old royal palace, telling how the deity Dorje Jono drove out a demon that brought drought to Lo. Reaching it needs a restricted-area permit and time to acclimatise.
body: Lo Manthang is the old walled capital of the kingdom of Lo, now Upper Mustang, at about 3,840 m on the Tibetan plateau side of the Himalaya. Tiji is its biggest public festival, held over three days each spring, usually in May, by the monks of Chode gompa in the town. The dances take place in the open square in front of the royal palace, inside the walls, and much of Upper Mustang comes in from the villages for it.

The festival tells one story over the three days. A demon has brought water shortage and disaster to Lo, and the deity Dorje Jono, born to defeat him, comes to drive him out. Masked dancers in brocade costumes act it out to drums, cymbals and long horns, ending on the third day with the demon's destruction and the return of order and rain to the land. The name is usually explained as a shortening of a Tibetan phrase about hope for the world's well-being.

For travellers, Tiji is the busiest time in Upper Mustang. Lodges in Lo Manthang fill, and you need the restricted-area permit arranged by a registered agency, a licensed guide and at least two trekkers in the group under current rules. The jeep road from Jomsom makes the trip possible in two days, but sleeping at 3,800 m without acclimatisation is a real risk. Dates follow the Tibetan calendar; check current status before you travel.
tips: Plan at least two nights on the way up, at Kagbeni or Chele and at Ghami or Tsarang, before the festival begins.
Book a Lo Manthang lodge months ahead and confirm it again close to the date.
Ask before photographing monks and dancers, keep off the dance ground, and never use a drone without written permission.

faqs.q: When is Tiji festival held in Lo Manthang?
faqs.a: Tiji runs for three days in the third month of the Tibetan calendar, which usually falls in May and sometimes late April or early June. The monastery fixes the dates each year. Check current status before you travel, then plan backwards: allow two or three days from Jomsom to reach Lo Manthang with sensible acclimatisation stops.

faqs.q: Do Indians need a permit to attend Tiji?
faqs.a: Yes. Upper Mustang is a restricted area, and Indian citizens, like other foreign nationals, need the restricted-area permit plus the Annapurna Conservation Area permit. The permit is issued through a registered Nepali trekking agency, with a licensed guide and at least two trekkers. Fees were changed in 2025; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How cold is Lo Manthang during Tiji?
faqs.a: Days in May are usually sunny and mild, around 12 to 20 °C, but the wind is strong from late morning and nights can fall close to or below freezing. Bring a down jacket, a warm hat, sunglasses, lip balm and high-factor sunscreen. The dance square has no shade, so a scarf for dust and sun helps.

faqs.q: Is altitude sickness a risk at Tiji?
faqs.a: Yes. Lo Manthang is at about 3,840 m, and driving up from Jomsom in a single day is too fast for many people. Sleep at Kagbeni or Chele and then Ghami or Tsarang on the way, drink water, avoid alcohol early and descend if symptoms worsen. Talk to your doctor before the trip about your health and any medication.
